  benchmark's 103 scores equal). Gate: `tests/test_memory_recall_reading_tag.py`
  (the tag after the value, the rule that left an unknown source untagged,
  and the hydrate without the source as negative controls).
- **A fact the user stated changes only in ways the user can see and take
  back** (2026-11, the audit's F1, second half; `memory/changes.py`, table
  `memory_changes` in `memory_state.db`). An **update**: a `user_*` fact
  replaced from another turn (`belief_mutation._mutate_functional_locked`,
  `users_fact_replaced`) is recorded by `changes.record_update` in the
  replacement's own transaction; `changes.undo` reopens the old fact and
  closes the new one under the mutation lock, audited (`undo_update`), and
  refuses with a code (`ChangeRefusedError`: `replaced_since`, `forgotten`).
  The model read one of the user's facts -- the one way a reading only the
  model made can become theirs -- with the value in the turn's own words,
  in a sentence that states it, with no one but the speaker named before it
  (`clause_subject.names_no_one_else`, the user's spelling: "We moved to
  Rotterdam", "Moved to Rotterdam last month", "No, Lisbon"; "My sister
  moved to Rotterdam" records nothing), from `_apply_beliefs_to_v2`
  (`_put_to_the_user`). A **pending change** -- a question -- only where the
  trust gate refused it over a fact the user stated (`changes.record_pending`;
  never over the user's words of the same turn). A **reading** (kind
  `reading`) -- never a question -- for the model's first reading of one of
  `fact_names.KINDS`, written as its inference (`changes.record_first_reading`):
  the deep pass files several facts on most turns, and a question the user
  ignores teaches nothing. The user confirms either (`changes.confirm`:
  written `user_explicit`, the change marked confirmed in that write's
  transaction, `mutate_belief(confirms_change=)`; a reading the model
  replaced since is refused, `replaced_since`) or dismisses it; "Not me" on
  a reading takes the model's fact out while it is current and still the
  model's (audited, `dismiss_reading`), and the deep pass never files that
  value again (`changes.user_said_not_me`; the newest `KEEP_NOT_ME`, 500 a
  tenant, are kept) -- the user's own words still can. Any fact the user
  states answers what is waiting on it (`changes.answer_pending`). One open
  change per value; an update supersedes them; one open 30 days
  expires; the newest 200 decided ones are kept per tenant. An update that
  closed the user's other list entries with its fact records them
  (`also_closed`), and undo reopens every one (the third review, item 4),
  except one whose value the user has said again since
  (`changes._held_again`, `_same_value`: it is current already; fix 5).
  **A memory tool follows rule A on replacement** (item 1): its subject and
  fact name are the model's even when the value is the user's, so its write
  passes `mutate_belief(replaces_users_fact=False)`; one that would replace
  a fact the user stated is put to the user as a pending change
  (`tool_builtins/memory._put_to_the_user`), one that only adds stays as it
  was. The model's "User" is the user (`fact_names.users_names`); a
  list-labelled value on a fact the user keeps single takes the user's
  row's class (`belief_mutation._established_kind`); the name table also
  reads "hometown", "location", "city", "current_location", "address",
  "moved_to", "first_name", "user_name" and other separators ("lives-in")
  (item 5). The turn's note is read at iteration 0
  (`changes.read_changes_note`) and marked told only after the model
  answered (`changes.mark_noted`): a failed call does not spend it (item
  6). An operator's API token may confirm a change: it can already edit
  facts at `user_explicit` (the main session's decision). Forget takes a
  change with the fact, the turn, the chat or the text it holds
  (`changes.forget_facts`, `forget_turn`, `forget_chat`,
  `forget_mentioning`); it is in the export and the M01 plant. The accepted
  cost of the speaker rule's sentence end ("صديقتي معلمة. ساكنة في جدة"
  read as the user's) is an update the user can undo. The Memory API
  answers them for the caller's tenant: `GET /api/memory/v2/changes`
  (`state` open or decided) and `POST /api/memory/v2/changes/{change_id}/confirm`,
  `.../dismiss`, `.../undo` (a refusal is its code, with the recorder's
  status: 404, 409); they are in the memory tenant gate's REQUESTS, from
  which Spaces S1-09 makes their matrix cases. The Memory page's card
  "Changes to what you told Kazma" (`memory_console.js` `loadV2Changes`,
  EN/AR, each value a `<bdi translate="no">`) shows them with Undo,
  "Yes, change it" / "No, keep it", or for a reading "This is right" /
  "Not me". In the chat apps `/memory changes`
  lists them with a short id (`changes.short_ref`) and `/memory undo|confirm|dismiss <id>`
  decides one (`changes.decide_change`: a unique start of the id, refused
  `ambiguous` or `wrong_kind`); the four words are a gateway admin's
  (`slash_commands.MEMORY_CHANGE_WORDS` in `changes_global_config`: they
  show and rewrite the tenant's facts). The next turn of the chat a change
  came from is told once: the supervisor adds the turn note
  `memory_changes` at iteration 0 (`changes.read_changes_note`, off the
  loop; the changes whose `source_session` is one of the thread's ids,
  marked `noted_at` by `changes.mark_noted` once the model answered; the
  values fenced, Kazma's lines outside).
  It asks little (`changes._to_tell`): every update, at most one question
  a turn, never about a fact asked about in the last day, never a reading;
  the rest wait on the page and in `/memory changes`.
  A turn of another thread -- a scheduled task, a sub-agent, an A2A
  request -- never spends it; the model cannot apply a waiting change
  (no tool decides one: a confirmation is the user's channel). Gates:
  `tests/test_memory_changes.py` (EN/AR; the refusal with no change log
  and every question in one note as negative controls), the plant's
  control in `tests/test_memory_store_registry.py`, and in a browser,
  reached by the sidebar, `tests/e2e/test_memory_changes_browser.py` (an
  undo, a confirmation and Kazma's reading answered, the database read
  after each, EN/AR).
- **A fact said to have stopped being true is ended, by the same rules**
  (2026-11-20, the framework audit's part C2, retractions). The deep pass
  may return a fact with `"ended": true` (strictly the JSON true), naming
  the held fact it ends ("replaces", F4's numbers) or matching a current
  fact of the same subject, same-words name and value
  (`belief_extractor._apply_ending`, `_current_fact`); it is never written
  as a new fact. `belief_mutation.end_belief` ends it under the mutation
  lock in one transaction (`valid_until` = when it was said; the mirror
  and graph copies follow from their outboxes), and the trust gate
  decides: the model's own reading ends at once, a fact the user stated
  answers `blocked: lower_trust_source`. That is put to the user
  (`changes.record_pending_end`) only when the value stands in the user's
  own words with no one else named (`clause_subject.ends_in_own_words`:
  `names_no_one_else` with the denial allowed, since an ending denies; a
  question, a quote or someone else's ending asks nothing). An ending is a
  change with no new value (`changes.is_ending`): "Yes, it ended" (confirm)
  ends the fact at the user's trust and records an ending update, which
  Undo reverses; the page ("Has this ended?", "Ended from what you said",
  "No longer: ..."; catalog `memory.console.change_*end*`, EN/AR), the
  turn note and `/memory changes` say it. The quick pass reads no endings:
  the user's own words are asked about, as a correction only the model
  reads. Gates: `tests/test_memory_retractions.py` (the ending ignored, and
  the statement rule on a denial, as negative controls), the write
  scenarios' `retraction` category, and `tests/e2e/test_memory_changes_browser.py`
  (an ending confirmed and undone on the page, EN/AR).
- The heuristic reads "I work at/for X" as `works_at` (it shared a pattern
  with "I live in" and stored the employer as `lives_in`), and the local
  embedder remembers short texts (<= 256 characters, 4,096 of them): each
  extraction with a fact re-embedded every entity name of the tenant.

**H2. Bring your history** (2026-11-14, REMAINING 4.2,
`memory/history_import.py`): a ChatGPT or Claude export (`.zip` or
`conversations.json`, read at most `MAX_JSON_BYTES`) becomes episodes through
`dual_write.write_episode` -- the ledger asked first, one vector, each turn at
its own time (`_LATE_WRITERS`), source `history_import` (after the fact:
episodic, never the working buffer), chat `import-<source>-<id>`. ChatGPT: the
`current_node` branch only, visible text only (no tool calls or output, hidden
instructions, images); Claude: `chat_messages` text. A turn already held is
skipped before it is embedded (re-import goes on where it stopped). No facts
(the deep pass calls the model). Surfaces: `kazma import` and the Memory
page's card (`kazma_ui/history_import_api.py`, admin, single-operator, one
import at a time, the upload deleted when it ends). Gates:
`tests/test_history_import.py` (real writer, recall after),
`tests/e2e/test_history_import_browser.py`.

**I. The user decides what is kept (U1, 2026-09-27, `memory/forget.py`).**
"Nothing lost" (F) guards against accidents; a user who takes a memory back
has decided otherwise, and every path that rebuilds memory must respect it.
- **Forgetting is a tombstone, never a delete.** The chat store still holds
  the conversation: a deleted episode would be re-created by turn reconcile,
  and one with its text gone looks erased to recovery. `forget_episode`
  empties question, answer and summary (`''`, never NULL -- NULL is what
  `rehydrate.ERASED_SQL` treats as erased, and it excludes tier `forgotten`
  too), drops the vector, sets tier `forgotten` (not in `RECALLABLE_TIERS`,
  no tier rule moves it), and does it to EVERY copy of the turn (the live
  write and reconcile use different keys of the chat).
- **The forget ledger** (`memory_forgotten`: tenant, chat key, turn number,
  question hash; turn 0 with no hash = the whole chat) is written under
  every key of the chat (`chat_keys`: session id and thread id, from the chat
  store). `dual_write.mirror_episode` asks it FIRST (`refuses_write`) -- it
  embeds, upserts the remote index and mirrors to Postgres even when its
  insert is ignored -- and so do the swarm bridge and the legacy restore.
  It asks under every id the chat has WHEN IT WRITES (2026-10-02): a web
  chat's thread id is saved with its first message, so a chat kept out
  before that has its row under the session id alone, and turn reconcile
  writes under the thread id; a test chat on live reached memory that way.
  Every product site that inserts an episode is declared in
  `tests/test_memory_forget.py`, and the live writers must ask the ledger.
- The facts a forgotten turn produced (`source_session`/`source_turn`) are
  invalidated and lose their subject, predicate, value, vector and every
  metadata field but where they came from (`forget._EMPTIED_FACT_COLUMNS`,
  `embedding = NULL`; an operator edit's `previous` goes with it; archived
  copies alike, `_scrub_archived_rows`). Subject and predicate were kept
  until 2026-11-21 (the memory framework audit's F5, part D: a forgotten
  "Sara was diagnosed with ..." read `sara` / `diagnosed_with` and the index
  answered "diagnosed"); `forget.finish_old_tombstones` empties older ones on
  the convergence pass. A forget cut short (`invalidate_belief` commits as
  it goes) is finished by asking again. The Postgres mirror gets the
  tombstones; the remote vector index loses the turn's AND its facts'
  vectors. Gate: `tests/test_forget_means_gone.py` (the word planted in a
  fact's subject, predicate and value; every kind of forget; restores;
  Arabic in two spellings; today's scrub, a case-only fold, an entry
  without ids or keys, and the old journal loop as negative controls).
- **Every copy is on one list** (`memory/memory_stores.py`, Memory audit
  M01, 2026-10-13): each table of `memory_state.db` and `memory_ops.db`,
  and each store outside them, with what Forget does there, its export
  section or why it has none, its retention and its bound. Forget reached
  the episode and the fact's value column only: the value stayed in the
  fact's vector and edit history, `beliefs_archive` (Hygiene and the
  180-day sweep), `memory_audit_log` (now redacted to a hash, the event
  kept), a queued turn's payload, the legacy tables, the full-text index
  segments (`purge_search_index`: FTS5 keeps a deleted row's words until a
  merge, and a merge on one level below the top keeps them too, so it
  goes through `db/fts5_purge.purge_deleted_rows`, §24 G) and
  `unified_items`, a copy of every fact and Knowledge chunk with
  no delete path that federated search served -- retired, dropped by
  `ensure_ops_schema`. A tool record keeps argument NAMES, never values
  (`procedural.strip_argument_values` rewrites older ones). What Forget
  cannot reach is the erasure horizon (`ERASURE_HORIZON`: backups, restic,
  exports, the pre-rebuild copy, freed SQLite pages, the Postgres dumps and
  WAL archive, Neo4j's transaction logs, migration bundles, the backup
  folder copy), said in the Forget dialog and the guide. Gates: `tests/test_memory_store_registry.py` (one
  word planted through every writer, forget, every column of every table of
  both databases read for it -- the forget of the day before and the
  missing purge as negative controls; every table declared, a planted one
  fails), `tests/test_memory_forget_witnesses.py` (the audit's witnesses,
  inverted).
- **Forget converges, and a restore does not undo it** (Memory audits
  M08/M10, 2026-10-13; `memory/forget_journal.py`). Every forget, keep-out,
  "remember again" and summary forget is appended to the forget journal
  (`<data dir>/memory_forget_journal.db`, its own file) BEFORE it changes
  anything -- a forget by text (`mentions`) and a turn kept out
  (`keep_turn_out`, a `turn` entry naming no memory) too since 2026-11-21 --
  and an entry of a chat records the chat's keys (`keys_detail`; a replay
  reads them with `entry_keys`: a chat forgotten and then deleted came back
  under its other key, since the store no longer named it); the memory
  database records what it applied
  (`memory_forget_applied`, inside it, so a restored older copy lacks the
  marks of later forgets). `forget_episode` runs EVERY step every time (the
  "already" path finished the facts only; summaries stayed active) and
  marks its entry applied only after the last one. The maintenance entry
  "forget convergence" (first of the memory sweeps, and at boot) applies
  pending entries in order; one that fails stays pending with every later
  entry of the same chat (a keep-out then "remember" must keep their order),
  and other chats' entries go on (it stopped at the first failure); memory
  health's "Forgets applied" check (`forget_journal.health`) warns when one
  fails or waits past a pass. It enforces the ledger on stored rows
  (`forget.enforce_ledger`: a forgotten turn's copy, a row written into a
  kept-out chat after the keep-out, a chat's past forgotten in the last day,
  an active summary from a forgotten turn) and retries remote deletes that
  failed (`forget_remote_pending`, also in the journal file). The writer's
  ledger check and insert are one `BEGIN IMMEDIATE`, and it pushes the row
  as it is now to the mirror and the remote index, never its arguments.
  Recovery and `scripts/scan_old_sessions.py` ask the ledger. A tombstone
  keeps a note's chat and turn (provenance, not content). The restore drill
  reports the forgets a backup would replay. Gate:
  `tests/test_memory_forget_converges.py` (a fault after each of ten steps,
  then one pass -> the M01 completeness scan passes; without the pass each
  leaves something; the three L05 witnesses inverted; a keep-out racing the
  writer on another thread; a pre-forget copy restored -> forgotten again,
  reconcile does not rebuild; negative control without the replay; only the
  forget code may pass `journal=False`).
- **"Don't remember this chat"** is the whole-chat ledger row: the writer
  refuses its turns, the post-turn worker (`_run_turn_memory`) extracts no
  facts, the past-chats search skips the chat -- and reads other chats
  without their forgotten turns. Web: the chat's menu (Memory...); chat
  apps: `/memory off` / `/memory on`. Turning it off also forgets what the
  chat left (`forget_past`).
- **What the agent stores with its memory tools belongs to the chat**
  (2026-09-27). `memory_store` and `memory_link_entities` name the chat and
  turn they run in (`tool_builtins/memory._chat_of_call`: the bound thread
  and `user_turn_index` of the turn's messages) -- on the note
  (`metadata.chat` / `chat_turn`) and on every fact (`source_session` /
  `source_turn`) -- and refuse in a chat kept out of memory. Forgetting a
  turn takes that turn's notes with it; forgetting a chat takes every note
  and every fact naming it (`_chat_notes`, `_forget_chat_facts`). Before,
  a test chat's token ("pebble-live") outlived the chat as a current fact.
  Gate: `tests/test_memory_tool_provenance.py` (every memory write in the
  agent's tool code names its chat).
- **`memory_store` writes only when the user asks to remember** (2026-11-22,
  the memory plan's finding 1, the main session's decision A). Its
  description opened "Use when the user shares personal info", so a fact the
  user simply told was kept twice -- the turn, which Kazma keeps and learns
  from, and the model's note -- and forgetting one copy left the other
  answering. Now it stores a note only when the running turn's latest user
  message, in the user's own words, asks to remember
  (`tool_builtins.memory._asked_to_remember`: `remember_request` through
  `own_words`, English and Arabic); anything else is refused before any
  store opens (`RefusedBeforeEffect`: "this turn is already remembered"). A
  swarm worker (no user message) is refused; a scheduled task's stored
  prompt is its turn's user message. Notes stored before are untouched.
  `memory_invalidate`'s description says to use it only when the user asks
  to forget or says a fact is wrong, never to record a change they told
  (finding 2). Gate: `tests/test_memory_store_only_when_asked.py` (EN/AR;
  today's tool as the control).
- **A swarm task's result follows the chat that started it** (2026-11-20,
  the framework audit's F10, part C2). The dispatch hands the task's
  conversation (`source_thread_id`, `worker_dispatch._source_chat`) and its
  space to `swarm_bridge.store_swarm_result(chat=)`: the result names its
  chat (`metadata.chat`), a chat kept out of memory stores nothing (the
  forget ledger asked for the chat too), and forgetting the chat takes it
  (`forget._chat_notes`, with no turn; a turn forgotten alone leaves it).
  A task no chat started is the worker's alone. Gate:
  `tests/test_swarm_results_follow_their_chat.py` (the dispatch without
  the chat, and a forget that does not look for results, as negative
  controls).
- **Compaction stores nothing in memory** (2026-09-27). Its summary was a
  second record of the chat under the session "compaction" and the tenant
  "default", out of reach of both controls above; every turn already
  reaches memory (F) and the weekly summaries hold the gist (J).
- **"About me" (C1, `memory/profile.py`)** is the user's own text (Settings
  → Memory, `GET/PUT /api/memory/v2/profile`, 2,000 characters, refused --
  never cut -- past that), one row per tenant in `memory_profile`, in the
  export. The supervisor reads it on every call (`get_about`, off the loop)
  and `graph_helpers._ensure_about_user` places it right after the system
  prompt and personality, replacing an earlier copy. Never inferred: a
  profile built from facts would have shown 4 past reset dates every turn.
  Changing it is admin-only under RBAC (`platform_rbac.role_allows`, Memory
  audit M11): it is guidance for every user of the tenant, like the
  personality. `tests/test_memory_about_me.py`, `tests/test_memory_tools_fenced.py`.
- **Kazma suggests About-me lines; the user decides** (2026-11, the memory
  framework audit's F13, decision 10; `memory/profile_suggestions.py`). A
  line ("I live in Porto.", "أسكن في الكويت.") is made only from a current
  fact the user stated themself (`provenance.USER_SOURCES`), never from
  Kazma's reading of a turn, a tool's fact or another member's words; in a
  shared space only from the asker's own entry, into the asker's own About
  me. It is written in the language the user said it in (the fact's turn,
  else the value's script), from a short table (`_LINES`). Nothing joins
  About me without the user's Add (`add_suggestion`: the line at the end,
  refused past the limit, never cut); Dismiss keeps it from coming back; a
  line already there is not offered. A decision is kept by the fact's id in
  `memory_profile_suggestions` (no value stored, so a forgotten fact leaves
  nothing to read). Routes: `GET /api/memory/v2/profile/suggestions`,
  `POST .../{belief_id}/add`, `.../dismiss`; the Memory page's card
  "Suggested for About me" (EN/AR). No model call. Gates:
  `tests/test_about_me_suggestions.py` (a suggester taking every source as
  the control), `tests/e2e/test_about_me_suggestions_browser.py` (by the
  sidebar, EN/AR).
- **Deleting a chat keeps its memories (S3, the owner's rule)** unless the
  dialog's "Also forget what Kazma learned from this chat" is ticked: then
  the page asks `PUT .../chats/{id}/memory {remember: false, forget_past:
  true}` FIRST (the forget finds the chat's other key through the chat
  store, which the delete empties) and deletes only if that succeeded.
  `tests/e2e/test_chat_delete_forget.py` (unticked makes no forget request).
- **Export** (`GET /api/memory/v2/export`, M22 2026-10-13): one section
  per `memory_stores` export section (`memory_api._EXPORT_QUERIES`; the
  export refuses to run when the two disagree) -- About me, facts, archived
  facts, every change to a fact, memories, weekly summaries, entities,
  entity merges, graph groupings, tool procedures, what was forgotten --
  and `not_included`, each table left out with why. A forgotten fact shows
  when, never what (no subject, predicate, chat or turn). Streamed, 500
  rows at a time, never built in memory. Gates in
  `tests/test_memory_store_registry.py` (every table with a tenant names
  its section or why not; a planted table and a section without a reader
  fail). The Memory page's "Memories of conversations" panel forgets one.
  **Every memory and weekly summary is reachable there** (Memory audit M23,
  2026-10-14): the panel listed the newest 30 memories and 40 summaries, and
  an older one could be forgotten only through the API. Both routes page
  (`offset`, `total`; the page shows "1–30 of N"), the memories route takes
  `q` (`routes_direct/memory._every_word_match`: every content word, each in
  any of its search forms -- recall's OR expression, newest first, filled the
  page with any memory sharing one word), and the probe's and "Search both
  stores" memory and summary hits carry Forget (`_forgetEpisode`,
  `_forgetSummary`, one dialog each). Gates:
  `tests/test_memory_forget_reachable.py` (every row reached page by page,
  the first page alone as the negative control; a list with Forget that
  loads without an offset fails), `tests/e2e/test_memory_forget_older.py`
  (the oldest of 35 forgotten through the page, English by paging, Arabic by
  search; ledger and tier checked).

**J. Weekly topic summaries (C2, 2026-09-27, `memory/topic_summaries.py`).**
Recall injects five turns and five facts; one topic on live ran to 100+
turns a week (ShipX 107 and 115, the fitness app's naming 108). Once a week
has ended (a day's grace), its turns are grouped by topic and the model
writes one summary per topic, on the durable queue (`topic_summaries`),
queued by the maintenance sweep with at most two weeks in flight.
- **Grouping, measured on live:** a chat with at least
  `memory.v2.summaries_min_turns` (4) turns in the week is one topic, under
  either of its keys (`chat_history.chat_ids`). Grouping every turn by
  meaning mixed chats: the question-first vectors of follow-ups ("recheck it
  again", "schedule them") say how the user talks, not what about, and an
  audit chat, a reminders chat and an X-posts chat became one group. The rest
  -- short chats, legacy single turns, the agent's notes (`memory_store`) --
  is grouped by meaning: average linkage, merging while the average
  similarity clears the tenant's own bar (the 90th percentile of pairs of
  its memories: 0.525 on live, the same from 200 to 1,676 memories; a
  week's own percentile split weeks of few topics). A question with fewer
  than two content words follows the previous turn of its chat. A V1
  migration copy of a turn memory also holds (`legacy-*`, "User: ...
  Assistant: ...": 181 of 269 on live) is left out -- the first run wrote
  three July topics twice. One rule decides what a copy is, here and in the
  live cleanup: `legacy_tables.legacy_copies`, the question AND the start of
  the answer (the migration cut answers at ~300 characters, "…"); the same
  question with another answer is another occasion. `forget.retire_copy`
  empties a copy without a ledger row and keeps its facts -- the original
  stays remembered, and the kept id stops the legacy restore bringing it
  back (`tests/test_memory_legacy_copies.py`).
- **Versioned:** a week done by an older `_VERSION` of these rules is
  summarized again, its summaries retired first; a forgotten summary stays a
  tombstone and still keeps its topic unwritten.
- **Derived, never a source:** `memory_summary_sources` names the turns.
  `forget.forget_episode` calls `on_turns_forgotten` before it commits: the
  summary is emptied at once (`rebuild`) and written again without the turn
  (`topic_summary_rebuild`), or retired below the minimum. A summary the
  user forgets is a tombstone its week never writes again (`_covered`: a
  topic mostly made of another summary's turns is that summary, even after a
  late turn joins it). The model's text passes `prompt_fence.filter_injection`
  and a credential mask. **The store is a compare-and-set** (`_store`,
  Memory audit M05, 2026-10-13): the model call takes up to a minute per
  topic, so inside one write transaction the source turns are read again --
  a text written from a turn forgotten meanwhile is never stored (the turns
  left, if still a topic, wait as `rebuild`) -- and a summary written again
  must still be `rebuild` (a forgotten one stays a tombstone). Until then a
  forget during the weekly run landed in an ACTIVE summary, and a rebuild
  overwrote a summary the user had just forgotten. A rebuild's store also
  cuts the summary's sources to the turns it was written from (2026-10-14:
  the forgotten turn's source row stayed, and `forget.enforce_ledger` sent
  the rebuilt summary back at every check, a model call each time). Gate:
  `tests/test_memory_summary_store_cas.py` (both witnesses inverted; every
  statement that sets a summary active names the status it replaces; the
  old store as negative control; the stale source row as the rebuild's).
- **Local only:** summaries live in the local memory database, like the
  graph, and are not mirrored to the Postgres state backend; they are
  rebuilt from turns. The Memory page's "Weekly summaries" panel lists and
  forgets them; memory health counts them.
- **Recall reads them (C2b)** on every path (the Postgres-primary one from
  the local database): every active summary of the tenant, ranked on
  evidence with the summary thresholds (`recall._SUMMARY_*`), at most two,
  shown AFTER the history ("## Weekly Summaries", week and title first, cut
  at 900 characters). The background is the MEDIAN of the question's
  similarity with every summary (`_summary_background`): bge-m3 puts a
  paragraph 0.14-0.19 below a turn, so the episodes' background sank true
  summaries below zero, and the episodes' "ranks 4-15" window fills with a
  topic summarized every week -- at 97 live summaries "list me all my
  subscription resets" (ten reset summaries) found none. Against the median
  every "catch me up" question of 23 real ones scored 0.235-0.439 and every
  unrelated one at most 0.170; floor 0.21. Benchmark v4 carries such a topic
  (eleven weekly training summaries): the ranks window hid the race result,
  the median finds it. Shown above the history, summaries pushed answering
  turns down (MRR 0.875 -> 0.868), so they come after it. Only `active` is
  ever recalled -- forgotten, `rebuild` (a forgotten turn's) and retired
  rows never are (`tests/test_memory_summary_recall.py`).
- Gate: `tests/test_memory_topic_summaries.py` (grouping identical to
  scipy's average linkage; each rule with a negative control).
- **Roll-ups above the weeks: a month, a project** (2026-11, the memory
  framework audit's F13, part G; `memory/topic_rollups.py`). A roll-up is a
  row of `memory_summaries` with its `level` (`week`, `month`, `project`),
  so recall, the page's list, Forget, the export and the space walk treat it
  as any summary. A month: its weekly summaries (a week is the month of its
  Monday), once the month has ended (a day's grace) and settled, at least
  `MIN_PARTS`. A project: weekly summaries that are one topic over at least
  `PROJECT_MIN_WEEKS` weeks, by average linkage at the tenant's own bar (the
  90th percentile of its summaries' pairs, never below `PROJECT_BAR_FLOOR`;
  measured on the benchmark: the training topic's 11 weeks are one group
  from 0.60 to 0.70). It names its sources twice: the weekly summaries in
  `memory_summary_parts` and their turns in `memory_summary_sources`. So a
  turn forgotten empties it (`on_turns_forgotten`, through the turns), and
  a weekly summary forgotten, retired or emptied empties it
  (`empty_rollups_of`, from `forget_summary`, `_retire`, `_retire_older`).
  The sweep (`queue_due_work` -> `plan_rollups`, at most six a pass) marks it
  `rebuild` with its parts; the queue's `topic_summary_rebuild` task writes
  it (`rebuild_summary` -> `rebuild_rollup`: one model call, the weekly
  summaries fenced), waiting while a part waits itself, retired below the
  minimum or when the model skips it. The store is a compare-and-set: every
  part still active and unchanged since it was read, the roll-up still
  waiting. A forgotten roll-up is a tombstone its month or project never
  writes again. Recall shows it under its own label (`rollup_label`:
  "October 2026", "Project, Sep 2026 to Nov 2026") and the block's header
  becomes "## Summaries"; a question about what was said in a period keeps
  the summaries of that period (`_summaries_in_time`, as part F keeps turns).
  A project is ranked as a weekly summary is, by its newest day
  (`period_end`), against the weekly summaries' background (a roll-up
  restates its weeks). A month's roll-up is a candidate only for a question
  whose period it overlaps (`_overlaps`): as a topic it held every topic of
  its month and was shown for "Where do I live?". A question that names
  nothing but talk and its time (`question_shape.asks_what_was_said`:
  "What did we talk about back in June?", "شنو تكلمنا عنه في يونيو؟") is
  answered by the period's month roll-ups by the share of it each holds
  (`_months_said_in`; by meaning June measured 0.08 against the floor of
  0.21), recorded in the benchmark's trace against a cut of nothing.
  Gates: `tests/test_memory_rollups.py` (a forget empties a roll-up built
  from it: through a turn and through a weekly summary; a roll-up that names
  no source, and a store without the re-read, as controls),
  `tests/test_memory_benchmark_rollups.py` (the dataset's roll-ups are the
  ones the planner makes; the `rollup` category with and without them;
  months ranked as topics, and the month questions by meaning alone, as
  negative controls). Dataset v7 (the `rollup` category, every v6 vector
  unchanged) was locked with `--rebaseline`: every v6 question scores the
  same or better on the v7 store; overall MRR and precision are lower only
  by the new category's (a summary is shown after the turns and facts).

**K. The Postgres memory mirror stays whole (2026-09-27, `memory/state_backend.py`).**
Found on live that day: 116 turns still "working" in the mirror (the
working-turn promotion never told it), 17 facts that never reached it, and 53
rows only the mirror held -- test data written before the database shield and
memories removed here since -- which recall's top-up could bring back into
an answer ("User prefers dark mode").
- **Every tier or text change reaches the mirror.** `remirror_episodes` is the
  one call after a local change (macro_sleep's moves, the working-turn
  promotion, forget, retire). Every `UPDATE episodes SET tier/text` in product
  code is declared with its path (`tests/test_memory_mirror_sync.py`, like
  the delete gate). `remirror_*_by_id` work on any connection (they used to
  need `row_factory = Row` and raised on the promotion's tuples).
- **The mirror sync** (maintenance entry "memory mirror sync",
  `sync_state_mirror`): compares the whole mirror with the local store -- id,
  tier and an md5 of the texts; for a fact, current or not and the value --
  and pushes what differs, newest first, at most 5,000 rows a pass
  (`_SYNC_LIMIT`; 500 while every push had its own connection), episodes in
  batches. A comparison still pushing with more behind is not stamped, so the
  next pass compares again (`catching_up`). A row only
  the mirror holds is counted (memory health `mirror`) and left alone, never
  deleted or copied back. Skipped with no mirror only: it runs when Postgres
  is the primary store too (2026-10-13, Memory audit M06) -- recall reads the
  mirror there, and a forget whose mirror write failed stayed whole in it for
  good. Digests match Postgres's own (real-Postgres test, Arabic, emoji,
  NULLs); NUL bytes are dropped on every mirror write.
- **A pass pushes what changed; the full comparison runs daily** (2026-10-14,
  Memory audit M31). Triggers (`schema_v2._ensure_mirror_outbox`) queue each
  episode or fact written, or changed in a column the mirror holds, in
  `memory_mirror_outbox` -- in the change's own transaction -- and a deleted
  fact (its mirror copy goes). The pass drains the queue (each row once, as
  it is now; a failed push retried 5 times, then left to the comparison; a
  row another region owns dequeued and counted, `outbox_conflicts`). The full
  comparison above runs once in `memory.v2.mirror_verify_hours` (24, 1-168;
  stamp `memory.v2.mirror_full_verify`, its findings kept in
  `memory.v2.mirror_verify_result`, both runtime). No mirror configured: the
  queue is emptied; configured but down: kept. A new mirrored column needs a
  trigger column -- `test_every_column_the_mirror_holds_queues_its_row` reads
  the upserts' SQL. Pushes go through a pool (`PostgresStateBackend._connect`,
  psycopg_pool, §44's `check=`) and in batches (`mirror_episode_rows`, 500 a
  batch, one region read per batch; `remirror_episodes` uses it and takes
  what it pushed off the queue, entries queued before its read only). Every
  row on its own connection, the first macro-sleep pass at 10x the live size
  took 336 s; batched, 7 s. **A mirror that went back is compared at once**
  (`_mirror_went_back`, 2026-10-14): a pass asks the mirror
  (`present_ids`) for the newest local rows it was already sent, and one
  missing (a `pg_restore` of an older dump) forces the full comparison, at
  most once an hour. The outbox had been drained for those rows, so recall
  on the primary path missed every memory since the dump until the daily
  comparison. Gates: `tests/test_memory_restore_drill_pg.py` (real Postgres,
  `pg_dump`/`pg_restore`; the incremental pass alone as the negative
  control), `tests/test_memory_mirror_incremental.py`. Measured limits (recall is the ceiling: 8 s a
  question at 170,000 memories) are in the guide, from the opt-in
  `tests/test_memory_scale_bench.py`. Gates:
  `tests/test_memory_mirror_incremental.py` (each with its negative control:
  a full pass reads both digests, a backend without batches pushes per row,
  the pool's connection count against a connection each, real Postgres).
- **Postgres-primary recall reads only what this install still remembers**
  (2026-10-13, M06). The mirror's keyword search and id fetch read only
  `RECALLABLE_TIERS`; the keyword channel orders by how many of the
  question's words a row holds (`words_held`), then by time -- it took the
  newest rows holding ANY word, so an older memory only its words would find
  fell out of the slice (the slice gate in `test_memory_nothing_lost.py`
  covers `state_backend.py`). Recall drops every row whose local copy is a
  tombstone or whose turn the forget ledger names (`recall._locally_forgotten`),
  whoever wrote it. Measured on the retrieval benchmark with the mirror as
  primary and the local vector index on the same vectors (the
  Postgres-primary keyword path, not pgvector): hit rate, MRR and precision
  equal to local (2026-11-21, dataset v8; `PRIMARY_DELTA`).
  The pgvector path is the other measurement (§15G, "pgvector in CI"). Gate:
  `tests/test_memory_pg_primary.py` (real Postgres: a forget with the mirror
  write failing, left out of recall, repaired by one pass; each with its
  negative control). The mirror tables are in `KAZMA_PG_TABLES` (§21A).
- **The primary path takes the local path's question-shape steps**
  (2026-11-21; CI's Postgres job was red from part F on, MRR 0.6889 against
  local 0.7133). After ranking, `_primary_episodes_as_local` and
  `_primary_beliefs_as_local` apply what `_recall_episodes` and
  `_recall_beliefs` do: the chat's own turns left out, the question's time
  (a period's turns and facts, or only them), the same text once, a list's
  compact lines and siblings, follow-ups joined to their turn. Candidates:
  a period's matches and turns from the mirror (`_primary_period_rows`;
  `search_state_episodes(between=)`, `state_episodes_between`) and a fact's
  earlier values from this install's database (`_primary_belief_rows`: the
  mirror keeps no chain of replaced values; a shared space's choice of whose
  facts too). A new step after ranking on the local path is added to both.
  Gates: the Postgres benchmark (without the steps as the negative control:
  CI's numbers) and, with no Postgres, `tests/test_memory_primary_parity.py`
  (a stand-in mirror over the same rows: every time, list, follow-up and
  roll-up question injects what local recall injects).
- **The top-up reads only other installs' rows.** Mirror writes carry the
  writer's install id (`metadata.install`, `<data dir>/install_id`);
  `written_elsewhere` admits a remote-only row only when another install
  wrote it. A row this install wrote and no longer holds was removed here;
  untagged rows (mirrored before the tag) count as this install's.
- **Region conflicts are counted, never pushed** (multi-region only). Under
  `origin_wins` a row another region wrote keeps its value quietly
  (`kept_by_origin`); under `fail_closed` the same refusal is reported
  (`region_conflicts`, a WARNING each pass, ops alert `memory.region_conflict`).
  The sync reads the writer's region (`row_regions`, a pattern read -- one
  malformed metadata row must not fail the query) and never spends the push
  budget on a refused row. The two policies behaved the same until
  2026-09-27. `tests/test_memory_mirror_sync.py`.

**K2. The Neo4j copy of the graph converges (2026-11-13, `memory/graph_sync.py`).**
`kazma setup install` sets Neo4j up by default since that day, and the copy
was kept by the dual-write alone (best effort, after the commit): a fact
written while Neo4j was down never reached it, an install with memories
before Neo4j was added had an empty one (the Settings button pushed the
first 1,000 current facts and removed nothing), a fact invalidated or
forgotten while it was down kept its edge -- and its value node -- for good,
and Neo4j down at a process's first fact made it use SQLite until a restart.
- **The sweep** "memory graph sync" (after the mirror sync,
  `run_graph_sync`), as the mirror's: triggers queue every fact written,
  changed in a column its edge depends on (`schema_v2.GRAPH_EDGE_COLUMNS`) or
  deleted, in `memory_graph_outbox` (`schema_v2._ensure_graph_outbox`), and
  each pass brings those facts' edges in step; a full comparison (every
  current fact against every edge of each tenant, Neo4j read first) runs
  daily, at once for a copy never compared or another Neo4j, one that went
  back (the newest facts it was sent are missing: recreated, restored),
  after a memory restore (`graph_sync.mark_full_due`, from
  `restore_memory_backup`) and while one is catching up. At most 2,000 writes
  and 120 s a pass, removals first, then the newest facts; a fact is read
  again just before its edge is written (a forget in between is not pushed
  back). Findings are the runtime setting `memory.v2.graph_sync`.
- **Only this install's edges change.** Every write carries the fact id and
  the install's id (the edge's install tag, `graph_backend.this_install`); an
  edge with no fact id, or another install's tag, is never written or
  removed (the dev checkout and live share one Neo4j at 127.0.0.1:7687), and
  an untagged edge of a fact this install never held is counted and left.
  The dual-write's upsert takes the same rule, and graph-clear deletes only
  this install's. Entity nodes left with no edge go. **Each install's facts
  have edges of their own** (2026-11-13): the write matches by install tag
  (`MERGE (a)-[r:TYPE {install: $inst}]->(b)`, `_UPSERT_EDGE`; a writer with
  no install id `_UPSERT_EDGE_UNTAGGED`), and another install's edge, or one
  with no fact id, at a key this install wants is counted (`held_elsewhere`)
  beside this install's own. Matched by type alone, the second install's
  write landed on the first's edge, so its fact left the graph when the
  first install forgot its own (until a daily comparison). A forget by id
  reads the subject's edges (`_DELETE_BY_ID_AT_KEY`, an index seek; by name
  until keyed), this install's only, never every edge of the database; the
  subject-object delete keeps to this install's too (`_THIS_INSTALLS_EDGE`).
  Gates: `test_real_server_two_installs_share_one_copy`,
  `test_real_server_a_forget_by_id_seeks_its_subject_and_keeps_to_this_install`
  and the type-only write as the control (`tests/test_memory_graph_sync.py`).
- **An outage is waited out:** one WARNING when Neo4j stops answering, one
  INFO when it is back, never a failed sweep; the queue keeps every change
  (100,000 at most, then a full comparison instead); no Neo4j chosen, it is
  emptied. No Neo4j call inside a memory write transaction (§15D2,
  `graph_sync._no_write_open`). The dual-write's SQLite stand-in for an
  unreachable Neo4j expires after a minute (`graph_backend._FALLBACK_RETRY_S`).
- **One implementation:** Settings -> Memory's "Sync beliefs -> Neo4j" runs
  a pass with the full comparison (`graph_sync.sync_now`; the old one-shot
  push is gone). Memory health shows the copy
  (`v2_health` graph entry's `copy`: in sync, behind N, unreachable, not
  configured), from the last pass, never asking Neo4j. The hygiene counts
  had replaced that whole entry since 2026-10-03, and the Memory page said
  "graph: sqlite" over a Neo4j store; they sit beside it now.
- **Nodes are found by key** (2026-11-13). With no index every write's
  `MERGE (:Entity {name, tenant_id})` scanned every Entity node: 500 rows over
  40,000 nodes took 8 s (neo4j 5.26). An index on `name` cannot hold a fact's
  value (Neo4j refuses an indexed value past ~8 KB; a value is up to 4,000
  characters, 16 KB in UTF-8) and a text index is not used by `MERGE`. So
  every node carries `key`, the SHA-256 of its name (`graph_backend.entity_key`,
  sent per row by `graph_backend.edge_row`), under the uniqueness constraint
  `kazma_entity_key` on `(tenant_id, key)` (Community has composite
  uniqueness; its index seeks every lookup, and `MERGE` locks its entry, so
  two writers of a new name make one node). Each pass keys the copy first
  (`graph_sync._key_nodes`): makes the constraint (read first with SHOW: the
  driver logs the notice `IF NOT EXISTS` answers, every pass; keys two nodes
  of a tenant share, written while there was none, are taken off all but the
  one with the most edges), keys every node with a tenant, a string name and
  no key -- never a node with no tenant -- streamed in one read
  (`graph_sync.KEY_STAMPS_PER_PASS` at most), each guarded by its name and
  "no key yet"; a keyless node whose keyed twin exists (an older writer made
  it after the switch) has this install's edges moved to the twin, written
  by key first and then removed, and goes once it has no edge; another
  install's edges stay, and the node is counted `held_elsewhere`. A pass
  that keys every node it can, the constraint there, records the copy
  `keyed` (`graph_backend.KEYS_KEY`, runtime, per Neo4j `target`); writes,
  `edges_at_keys`, `neighbors` and `delete_triple`'s subject-value branch then
  find nodes by key (the backend reads the record at most every 30 s; the
  sync's own process at once). Until then, and after any pass that cannot
  finish (time, a refusal, an outage), it is `transitional`: nodes are found
  by name, which is right in every state -- a new node gets its key when it
  is made, only (setting a found node's key would be refused when its keyed
  twin exists). Of two edges at one key the one between keyed nodes stands
  (`Held.keyed`). Memory health says whether the copy is keyed and how many
  nodes still have no key. Measured on neo4j 5.26 with 40,000 Entity nodes
  (three runs each): 500 rows in one statement 8.4-8.7 s -> 0.07-0.19 s, 500
  dual-writes 7.7-9.0 s -> 0.8-0.9 s; keying the 40,000 took 5.5-5.9 s.
- Gate: `tests/test_memory_graph_sync.py` (an in-memory Neo4j answering the
  backend's statements, the product's writers; each case shows the copy as
  the old code left it first; a real-server case with
  `KAZMA_TEST_NEO4J_URL`, never this machine's 7687 unless
  `KAZMA_TEST_NEO4J_THROWAWAY=1`). For keys: one node per name through
  every phase with writes between, an old writer after the switch converging
  in one pass, a 4,000-character value of 4-byte characters, the plan an
  index seek (EXPLAIN), foreign edges and nodes with no tenant unchanged, two
  concurrent writers of a new name; negative controls: switching before
  every node is keyed duplicates, the keyed write over a plain index (and
  the write before keys) duplicates under concurrency, an index on `name`
  refuses the value. One real-server test drops and remakes
  `kazma_entity_key`.

**L. The graph shows what memory holds, and extraction keeps it clean
(2026-10-03, `memory/graph_view.py`, `entity_retire.py`, `graph_hygiene.py`).**
On live, the Memory graph showed many nodes alone; most were made by the
drawing, the rest by extraction.
- **The route cuts by connected group** (`graph_view.keep_connected`): the
  hub's group grown out from the hub by belief count, then the other groups
  by weight. A node kept without the neighbours that join it to its group is
  painted alone, and the old sort-and-slice dropped the one-belief fact
  nodes first. The hub links of every endpoint (`user → related_to → X`,
  importance 1) are loaded past the 800-fact cap: the cap ranked them last
  and dropped them first. A literal value (`true`, `4`) is one node per fact
  (`value:<belief id>`, `isValue`), never dropped and never one shared node.
  `stats.isolated` counts nodes alone in the DATA, before the cut.
- **A vector auto-merge leaves a redirect** (`entity_resolution._auto_merge`):
  the merged name becomes a shell with `metadata.merged_into`, and the
  target gains the name's alias hash. The ledger row named an entity that
  did not exist, so under `ensure_primary_schema`'s foreign keys every
  auto-merge raised (logged at DEBUG) and created a duplicate. Quarantine
  creates the new entity before its ledger row for the same reason. The
  extractor files a fact under the id a name resolved onto.
- **An entity's id keeps its script** (`entity_resolution.slug`, the ONE
  id rule, Memory audit M02, 2026-10-13): NFKC, casefolded, the letters,
  marks and digits of every script, other runs one `_`, 80 characters; an
  id for a label with no letter (an emoji) from its own text; an empty label
  has none (`ValueError`; `mutate_belief` refuses it). The rule kept
  `a-z0-9` and fell back to `"entity"`, in four copies plus the Memory
  API's: every all-Arabic, Persian or CJK subject was `entity`, unrelated
  facts superseded each other, and later non-Latin objects were rewritten to
  `entity`. ASCII ids are unchanged. Spellings that differ by vowel marks or
  letter forms meet in the alias hash (`documents.arabic.fold_for_search`),
  never in the id. An id is a tenant's: the key is `(tenant_id, id)` (M21,
  §16's multi-tenant note), and a redirect (`canonical_entity_id`), a
  protection (`entity_protection`), a count and a retire read the tenant's
  own row. Service names (`current_facts`) and the same-words key
  (`graph_hygiene`) use it too. Rows the old rule wrote: `entity_repair`
  (`scripts/memory_entity_repair.py size`, then `apply` on a copy) quarantines
  each collapsed fact and queues its turn for the deep pass -- nothing is
  guessed; the live run is the owner's. Gate: `tests/test_memory_entity_ids.py`
  (Arabic, Persian, CJK, emoji through the writer and the extractor; no
  `a-z0-9` keep-list or `"entity"` fallback in memory code, the old rule as
  the negative control; the repair on a copy).
- **Tier-2 resolution queries stored name vectors** (2026-10-13, Memory audit
  M18): an entity keeps its name's vector (`entities.embedding`, stored at
  creation, by `_store_name_vector` on an exact match, and by the vector
  repair pass for older rows, `repair_entity_name_vectors`), and
  `resolve_entity` asks `VectorEngine.nearest_entities` for the nearest. Every
  extraction embedded every entity name of the tenant (93 names, seconds of
  CPU a turn on live; past 4,096 names the short-text cache thrashed). An
  extraction now embeds only the names it resolves. Gate:
  `tests/test_memory_entity_name_vectors.py` (the same embed calls at 60 and
  6,000 entities; the old scan as the negative control).
- **Subjects that are work items are not entities**
  (`ego_anchor.subject_should_mint_entity`: phases, tickets, versions,
  hashes, paths, mostly-digit and sentence-length slugs). The fact is still
  written and anchored. An object is minted only beside a subject that is
  an entity. The deep pass is given the subjects in use
  (`entity_resolution.entity_vocabulary`), as it is given the predicates.
  A ticket has three digits at least: slugs are lower case, so "gpt-4",
  "windows-11" or "covid-19" look like tickets by shape, and a product
  losing its node costs more than a ticket keeping one. Measured on live
  (377 entities) the rules matched six, all clutter.
- **An entity goes with its last fact if it holds nothing else**
  (`entity_retire.retire_empty_entities`, from `invalidate_belief` and a
  supersede): a plain concept only -- own name and hash as aliases, no
  metadata, grouping, merge row or redirect onto it; not protected, major
  or high-stakes. Declared in `tests/test_memory_deletes.py`.
- **Which entities no delete, merge or purge takes is one answer**
  (`memory/entity_protection.py`): core ids (`user`, `assistant`, `kazma`),
  the hub's own names (`self_hub.collect_self_entity_ids`: an entity the
  hub's aliases name, or one labelled you/me/user) and the operator's flag.
  A self entity may still be merged INTO the hub. Five copies did not agree,
  and four named Kazma's author: every install protected an entity called
  "mubder" and none its own owner's other names. A store that cannot answer
  refuses (the page's check answered "not protected" on a read error). Every
  purge (the page's Hygiene, `memory_purge_empty_entities`) removes exactly
  `entity_retire.plain_empty_shells`, and memory health's `empty` counts
  that list: both purges deleted every entity with no live fact, merge
  redirects included, and a redirect is how a merged name keeps reaching
  its target (`canonical_entity_id`). Gates:
  `tests/test_memory_entity_protection.py` (an install whose owner is
  Layla; the old purge rule as the negative control) and
  `tests/test_no_owner_identity_in_product.py` (no product string literal
  names the author, none outside a docstring the author's projects; the
  repository's address is the product's).
- **The page's counts converge** (`entity_counts.repair_entity_counts`,
  maintenance entry "entity count repair"): an entity whose stored
  `belief_count`/`graph_degree` differ from the live counts is recomputed,
  500 a pass, and a merge recomputes the neighbours too
  (`recompute_entity_counts(neighbours=True)`: one that linked to both
  names has one neighbour fewer). 11 of 377 live entities were wrong, two
  since an August merge. The stats bar's "empty" is what the purge takes,
  and a redirect is listed "merged into X", never "empty" -- the bar
  counted redirects and stayed above zero after a purge.
  `tests/test_entity_count_repair.py` (the source-and-target-only
  recompute as the negative control).
- **The Memory page says what happened** (2026-10-13, Memory audit M32):
  hygiene is `ok` only when every action it ran is (`failed`, `error:
  hygiene_partial`; it said "Hygiene complete" over a failed archive); the
  Episodes chip counts `RECALLABLE_TIERS` only (it counted tombstones); the
  archive of ended facts returns `remaining` and its `cap` (2,000 a run, said
  in the label and the toast); a forget whose remote vector delete is pending
  says so; the probe panel shows weekly summaries and a degraded search;
  server messages the page shows are codes (`not_found`, `protected`,
  `about_too_long` with `length`/`max`) worded by the page in its language.
  Gates: `tests/test_memory_page_truth.py`,
  `tests/e2e/test_about_me_limit_arabic.py`.
- **The Memory page is laid out by what a person comes for** (2026-11-19,
  the owner's request after the 2026-11-18 review): status, the memory map,
  what Kazma knows, conversations; the clean-up and the health numbers are
  folded (`#memory-cleanup`, `#memory-health`, `components/memory_health.html`).
  Its words are the catalog slice `i18n/catalog/memory_page.py` (EN/AR).
  **Restore takes only a backup of the memory database**: the list showed the
  operations database's copies (`memory_ops_<ts>.db`) beside the memory
  ones with the same Restore button, and restoring one replaced every memory
  with the task queue. The list and the route take only
  `backup.is_memory_backup_name` (`memory_state_<ts>.db`, the stem of
  `primary_memory_db`), and `restore_memory_backup` refuses a file without
  the memory database's own tables (`NotAMemoryBackup`, read `immutable=1`)

- **Memory input is bounded and escaped** (2026-10-13, Memory audit M36): one

- **The Entities search finds an entity by its id**

- **Memory health reports the clutter** (`v2_health` -> `graph`: empty,

**M. Running it: what recall did, the pages it raises, the search past a
size, the sweeps' cursors, and the person's own view** (2026-11-21, the
memory framework audit's part H, findings F14 and F15; no model calls).
- **One recall record per turn** (`memory/recall_records.py`, table
  `memory_recall_records` in `memory_ops.db`): the supervisor's iteration-0

- **Three pages, each once per outage, each with its recovery**

- **Search past a size narrows, then scores exactly**
  (`memory/vector_codes.py`). Exact search stays the truth: a sign code

- **Every memory sweep has a budget and a cursor** (`memory/sweep_cursors.py`,

- **What Kazma knows about you** (`/memory/you`, `memory/about_you.py`,

- **The Memory page's quick recall check** (it was "golden eval",

### 16. Scheduled reminders and tasks (`kazma-core/kazma_core/cron/`)

The agent's `schedule_task` / `list_scheduled` / `edit_scheduled` /
`cancel_scheduled` (native `task_scheduler_cron`) and the Scheduled page
(`/scheduled`, `kazma_ui/scheduled_api.py`) → `CronScheduler`
(`cron/scheduler.py`) → `SQLiteCronStore` (`cron/store.py`,
`kazma-data/cron.db`). X posts on the same page are the X publication
store's operations (§29C). Hardened 2026-10-14 against the Scheduled audit
(`docs/audits/AUDIT_SCHEDULED_2026-10-13.md`, tracker
`docs/plans/SCHEDULED_INDUSTRIAL_HARDENING_GOAL.md`; the 7-day fake-clock
soak's harness is built, I; the run itself is still open). Every rule below
must hold:

**A. The scheduler MUST be constructed with a `graph_builder=`.**
`app.py` builds `CronScheduler(store=…, graph_builder=_cron_graph_builder,
poll_interval=…)`. The closure returns `cron_fire_graph(agent,
capabilities=…)` (`cron/capabilities.py`): the agent's one-shot
`build_child_graph(declared_tools=…)` (checkpointer=None). Without it a
task's fire fails -- counted and alerted, never delivered. A reminder needs
no graph.

**A2. A fired job does only what it declared** (decision D12, SCH-S05).
`kind="reminder"` (the tool's default) delivers its stored text with NO
model call. `kind="task"` runs an agent turn offered exactly its declared
tools: `read` (read-tier tools, the default) or `read_write` (the write
tier too); MCP and `ALWAYS_HITL` tools never. `DeclaredToolExecutor`
refuses a call to anything else, and the job's one delivery is the
scheduler's, not a tool. The prompt reaches the model labelled as a stored
instruction. The booking's approval card says what the job will do, and an
edit's card shows the prompt now and after (`cron/card.py`). A task does
not fire while HITL is off unless the operator set
`safety.cron_fire_without_hitl` (the agent cannot: `safety.` is protected,
§45). Gate: `tests/test_cron_capabilities.py` (the old builder's whole
registry as the negative control).

**A3. Ready-made automations** (2026-11-14, REMAINING 4.3,
`cron/recipes.py`): a recipe is an ordinary `task` with `capabilities="read"`
(days fixed, time chosen, the page's language), booked by the Scheduled page's
own path (`scheduled_api` `_book`, which the page's form uses too: delivery
address, zone, outbox, approval card all apply). The `read` set includes the
`safe` tier (email reading: `side_effects` and the MCP server already count
it as read), never `email_send`/`email_delete`/`email_categorize`. Gates:
`tests/test_automation_recipes.py` (the real scheduler; every recipe a card
and words), `tests/test_cron_capabilities.py`
(`test_a_read_task_reads_email_and_never_sends_it`, the old read set as the
control), `tests/e2e/test_automation_gallery_browser.py`.

**B. `delivery_target` is captured at schedule time, not resolved at fire time.**
`schedule_task` reads `get_current_delivery_target()` (the
`_current_delivery_target` ContextVar, bound at the gateway handler entry
AND re-set in the tool-worker node from the `_gateway` routing block —
same two-layer pattern as `_current_thread_id`) and stores it on the job.
At fire time the job's own target is used. A job whose target is empty or
malformed adopts a sibling job's target on the same thread (and keeps it),
then tries the thread's session -- best effort only: sessions TTL-evict
after 5 min, so no reminder may rely on it. With none, the delivery is
`undeliverable` at once, with an alert naming the job; nothing goes to a
guessed address (the old `"{platform}:unknown"` fallback is gone). No tool
result or page answer carries the address: `ScheduledJob.to_dict()` gives
`destination`, a label (SCH-S10). The platform-isolation invariant (§2) is
preserved — `chat_id` never enters graph state; `delivery_target` joins
`thread_id`/`platform` in the internal `_gateway` routing sub-dict.

**B2. A web turn's delivery target is for reminders, not for answers.**
`web_gateway_block` stamps the operator's Telegram as a web turn's
`delivery_target` so a reminder booked on the web rings somewhere. A tool that
answers INTO the conversation reads the conversation's platform
(`send_message.get_current_platform()`, bound beside the delivery target in
the tool worker), never the delivery target alone: `send_file` did, and a web
chat's files went to Telegram while the answer said "sent to this chat"
(2026-09-28). On a web turn `send_file` and `generate_image` share a copy into
the chat (`kazma_core/chat_files.py`, `<data dir>/attachments/shared/`),
served by `GET /api/chat/files/{id}` to that chat's owner only (raster images
inline, everything else a sandboxed download) and shown through the Markdown
the tool hands the model. `tests/test_web_chat_files.py`.

**C. The store's connection is autocommit (2026-09-27).** `SQLiteCronStore`
opens cron.db with `isolation_level=None`, so every statement is its own
transaction. In Python's default mode a DELETE opens a transaction even when
it matches nothing, and the purge (at start and hourly) committed only when
it had deleted something: from each boot until the next reminder fired the
server held cron.db's write lock, and the live-data cleanup stopped half way
with "database is locked". A group of writes (a claim, a fire's finish, a
delivery's outcome) is one `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` through
`db.sqlite_session.write_transaction`. Gates:
`tests/test_cron_store_write_lock.py` (every public method, then another
connection must take the write lock at once) and §35's kept-connection gate.

**D. A fire is a durable, leased record, and ends once** (SCH-E04, E01,
E07). A fire claims its job by compare-and-swap (`claim_job`: pending →
running, with `fire_owner`, `lease_until`, `fire_due`, `fire_attempt` and
the version it read). Its result, a recurring job's next occurrence, the
job's status and the delivery row then commit in ONE transaction
(`finish_fire`). A crash anywhere leaves either nothing (the fire runs
again) or a finished fire whose delivery the outbox owns. Recovery decides
per phase. At boot every running row belongs to a dead runtime and goes
back to pending at the same occurrence; it used to be marked FAILED,
delivered or not. While running, a row past its lease, or ours with no
task, goes back the same way. A failed agent turn (an exception, `error`,
`turn_failed`) is a failed fire: counted and alerted (`cron.job_failure`;
`cron.job_failed` when its budget of 3 runs out), never delivered as the
reminder. A task's turn runs in its fire's own task, under
`asyncio.timeout` (§9: on Python 3.11 `wait_for` gave it a task of its own,
which a second cancel left running). Shutdown stops cron first and drains
fires within a bound; `/health/activity` counts them (`active_fires`), and
`kazma_guard.py --reload --when-idle` waits for them. Retention purges by
`finished_at`, and recovery reads every running row. Gates:
`tests/test_cron_fire_record.py`, `tests/test_cron_crash_matrix.py` (a real
child killed at each phase, one-off and daily: exactly one delivery, or one
honest state with an alert; the old RUNNING→FAILED recovery is the negative
control).

**E. Delivery goes through a leased outbox, acknowledged only on `sent:`**
(SCH-E02, §51). `cron_deliveries` holds a row per message. It is claimed
with a lease, retried with backoff (30 s doubling to 15 min, at most 6
attempts within 2 hours), and acknowledged only when `send_message`
answers `sent:`. A refused delivery ends `undeliverable` -- the job too,
never DONE -- with exactly one alert (`cron.delivery_failed`). A row whose
sender died mid-send ends `unknown` (`delivery_unknown` on the job, alert
`cron.delivery_unknown`) and is never sent twice. The job, the page and the
daily digest show the outcome. Gate: `tests/test_cron_delivery_outbox.py`
(the old deliver-then-finalize order is the negative control).

**E2. Alerts go through an outbox too** (2026-10-15, found by the Stage 5
soak). A change that needs an ops alert writes its `cron_alerts` row in its
OWN transaction (`SQLiteCronStore._enqueue_alert`, called only inside
`self._tx()`): a failed fire or a budget run out in `finish_fire`
(`cron.job_failure` / `cron.job_failed`), a message ended undeliverable in
`finish_delivery` (`cron.delivery_failed`), a send recovered `unknown` in
`recover_deliveries` (`cron.delivery_unknown`). The scheduler drains it after
the commit -- after a fire, after a delivery pass, at each poll and at start
(`CronScheduler._drain_alerts`) -- into `ops_alerts.alert` (§33: no fourth
notifier), and marks a row sent only after `alert` returned. A crash after the
commit loses nothing; a crash between the alert and its mark raises it once
more, the only duplicate. One pass at a time, a row whose mark failed is
marked next pass without being raised again, and `stop()` waits for a pass in
progress before it cancels. A row `ops_alerts` cannot raise stays queued with
a WARNING and a backoff (`kazma_cron_alerts_pending` on /metrics,
`alerts_pending` in readiness). Raised rows follow the job retention; one not
yet raised is kept. A missed occurrence alerts only through its notice's
delivery. Until then a delivery's alert was marked before it was raised and a
fire's was raised after its commit: a crash in either window lost it. Gate:
`tests/test_cron_alert_outbox.py` (a real child killed in each window of each
gap, the old order as the negative control; the cron engine names
`ops_alerts.alert` only in `CronScheduler._raise_alert`; no alert row outside
its change's transaction). The soak kills in both windows and counts the
recorded duplicates (`scripts/scheduled_soak.py`, `alert_redelivered`).

**F. Missed is missed** (SCH-E06). A job due longer ago than its catch-up
window does not run. The window is `cron.catchup_minutes` (default 60), or
`KAZMA_CRON_STALE_HOURS` when that is unset; a window given at booking wins
over both. The job is `missed` (a recurring job moves on to its next
occurrence), and its chat gets ONE notice through the outbox. A late fire
inside the window says how late ("(due 09:00 Asia/Kuwait, 12 min late)").
X posts keep their own 5-minute hold (§29C). Gate:
`tests/test_cron_fire_record.py::test_each_lateness_band`.

**G. One timing model, in the operator's zone** (SCH-E03, E05, E09;
`cron/timing.py`). A naive time means `cron.timezone` (else `KAZMA_TZ`,
else UTC) on every path: chat, the Web form, `edit_scheduled` and X
booking resolve one string to one instant. It accepts `5m`/`2h`/`3d`,
RFC 3339 (`Z` and offsets honoured), and a typed recurrence: daily,
weekdays or weekly at a clock time, or an RRULE subset (FREQ daily/weekly,
BYDAY, BYHOUR/BYMINUTE, UNTIL/COUNT, TZID). It refuses, naming the zone:
the past; more than two years ahead (`MAX_HORIZON`); more than 100
characters; and a one-off inside a clock change's gap or fold. A recurring
job takes the earlier time of a fold and shifts across a gap. X booking
takes one-offs only. The commitment gate (§20) never rewrites a recurrence,
and rewrites a one-off only to an aware instant in that zone; a recurring
request booked as a one-off is refused. Gate:
`tests/test_cron_timing_model.py`. It runs one fixture in UTC, Asia/Kuwait,
America/New_York and Europe/London, a daily series across two clock
changes, and checks that every docstring, manifest and hint example is
accepted by its validator.

**H. Only legal actions, and the stored truth** (SCH-E12, S02, S07, S04).
The statuses are pending, running, delivering, done, failed, cancelled,
undeliverable, missed and delivery_unknown.
- Edit and cancel carry the version the form read; a stale one is 409
  `conflict`. During a fire they are recorded and applied when it ends
  (202 `edit_pending` / `cancel_pending`).
- A finished job comes back only through Restore
  (`POST /api/scheduled/cron/{id}/restore`).
- The page offers only what the server lists in a job's `actions`. Its
  dialog fetches the full prompt and sends only the changed fields, so a
  timing edit never touches the prompt.
- The page's X rows are the publication store's operations, changed through
  `/api/x/queue/{op}/reschedule|cancel`. The page's own X PUT/DELETE routes
  are gone.
- Every change records its actor and source (`cron_events`).
- The API and the page share one status-class map
  (`tests/test_scheduled_presentation.py`).

Gates: `tests/test_scheduled_api.py` (real scheduler and store),
`tests/test_cron_fire_record.py::test_state_by_action_matrix`,
`tests/js/test_scheduled_page.js`.

**I. One operator, bounded, off the loop** (SCH-S03, E14, E10, E11, S12).
- **Single operator:** on an install with platform users every Scheduled
  surface refuses (decision D1, `cron/single_operator.py`). The routes answer
  409 `scheduled_single_operator`, the page shows a banner, the tools give the
  reason. In production mode reads and changes keep to the caller's tenant;
  another tenant's id reads as unknown.
- **Bounds:** 500 jobs a tenant and 50 a thread (Settings keys
  `cron.max_jobs_per_*`); a prompt of 8,000 characters and a timing of 100; a
  `scheduled` rate bucket (30 a minute); a task turn's budget
  (`cron.task_budget_seconds`).
- **Throughput:** a pass reads up to `max(50, max_concurrent * 10)` due
  jobs and starts them all; the semaphore holds all but `max_concurrent`.
  50 jobs due among 1,000 fire in one pass
  (`tests/test_cron_load.py`; the old four-a-pass rule is the negative
  control).
- **Off the loop:** the zone, the tenant rule, the address and the graph build
  are resolved in a thread (static gate area `scheduled`,
  `tests/test_scheduled_off_loop.py`).
- **Readiness and metrics:** readiness reads the poll heartbeat
  (`CronScheduler.liveness()`), degraded once the heartbeat is older than
  two poll intervals plus 30 s. /metrics carries fires, missed jobs, lateness p50/p95, the
  outbox and the heartbeat. The digest counts outcomes from the
  `[cron] outcome` line (`tests/test_cron_liveness.py`).
- **Dates and origin:** dates on the page and in X Studio go through
  `KazmaFormat`. `kazma_ui/same_origin.verify_same_origin` is the one
  same-origin check for the Scheduled, X and email routes.
- **Qualification soak:** `scripts/scheduled_soak.py` (Stage 5) runs the real
  scheduler and store on a private cron.db through seven simulated days of a
  fake clock -- the engine reads every time and its poll wait from one
  `CronClock` (`cron/clock.py`; gate `tests/test_cron_clock.py`) -- with
  thousands of jobs, injected provider, delivery and database failures and
  restarts, and checks each due occurrence against its own ground truth
  (`tests/test_scheduled_soak_harness.py`: a short run, and planted losses as
  negative controls).

**Multi-tenant memory:** tenants are enforced with
`KAZMA_MEMORY_ENFORCE_TENANT=1`, in production (`KAZMA_PRODUCTION=1`) and with
multi-user on (`memory.config.memory_tenant_enforced`, the one answer for
turns and surfaces). **Turns and surfaces resolve the same tenant** (Memory
audit M07, 2026-10-13): under enforcement both are the principal's tenant in
every mode (`resolve_tenant_id` wrote shared-mode turns to "default" while the
page looked in the principal's), and only `shared` can be saved
(`settings_validation`, key `memory.config.TENANT_MODE_KEY`); not enforced,
the page keeps the install's own view, and its "Don't remember" ledger rows
and About me (`profile.about_for_turn`) reach every tenant's turns. The chat
delete says when there was nothing to forget. Gate:
`tests/test_memory_tenant_matrix.py` (mode x enforcement x principal; the old
resolver as negative control). Then every `/api/memory` route
reads, counts and changes only the request tenant's rows -- another tenant's
id reads as not found (`memory_api._row_tenant_ok`,
`hygiene.invalidate_belief(tenant_id=)`) -- and the engine's own maintenance
(task queue, reconsolidation, golden eval) is admin-only
(`platform_rbac._ADMIN_PREFIXES`). The install's own tenant (`default`: no
binding) is the install's view (`_tenant_clause`) only while Spaces is not
enforced; once it is, `default` is the owner's space and reads its own rows
(§70, `memory/tenant_view.py`). Gate:
`tests/test_memory_routes_tenant_scope.py` -- every route, enumerated from the
app, called as one tenant with another's ids; nothing of the other shown or
changed, and the caller's own rows shown. **Entities are keyed by
`(tenant_id, id)`** (Memory audit M21, 2026-10-15, `memory/entity_key.py`):
each tenant holds its own row of an id -- its own `kazma`, its own `user` hub
(`self_hub.ensure_user_hub` writes the caller's) -- and `entity_merges` names
its entities by the pair (composite foreign keys). Every statement on
`entities`, `entity_merges` or `entity_merges_archive` names its tenant, and
one that picks a row by id names it in that WHERE; a statement that reads
across tenants on purpose is declared with why. Which row a request means is
one answer, `entity_key.entity_owner`: a tenant's own; the install's view
(`default`) its own first, else the one tenant holding the id (several, and
none of the install's: not found). A merge keeps to the source's tenant (a
target of another tenant is not found), and the belief rewire and the ledger
row are that tenant's. A store made before then keeps the `id` key until the
operator runs `scripts/memory_entity_key.py` (`size` reads only; `apply --db
--yes` copies to `<db>.pre_entity_key` first, then rebuilds both tables in one
transaction -- every row, id, tenant and rowid kept, the search index rebuilt
-- idempotent); every statement works on both keys (on the old one the
2026-10-13 rules hold the boundary: creation never writes another tenant's
row, rename promotes only a node of the caller's own facts, an id another
tenant holds and an unused one both answer not_found), and memory health says
which key the store has (`entity_key`). The Postgres mirror holds facts and
memories, never entities. Gates: `tests/test_memory_entity_key.py` (the source
gate, planted old statements as its control; two tenants holding one id
through every memory route, enumerated from the app, and every agent memory
tool, from the registry, with an owner lookup answering the other tenant and
the old key as negative controls; the migration on a copy of a store the
product's writers seeded under the old key, then recall, the graph and a
merge; the script), `tests/test_memory_entity_tenancy.py` (the four witnesses
inverted).

### 17. Lifecycle Status Notifier (`kazma-core/kazma_core/lifecycle_notifier.py`)

Server lifecycle status notifications — ONE card per boot (2026-09-29, the
owner's request: a reload sent three messages, and the restart card named the
adapters without saying whether any had connected), plus a card when startup
fails. The start card waits for the chat apps and says how long Kazma was
down (or that the last run did not shut down cleanly), each adapter ✅ or ❌
with the connection's reason, the build and the model. Four invariants:

**A. Notifications route through the SwarmMessageBus — no parallel path.**
`notify_lifecycle(event)` sends a `BusMessage` through the adapters
selected by `notifications.ops.channels` (same Settings checkboxes as
ops alerts; empty = every configured platform). `bus_send_targets()`
filters a `FanOutBusAdapter`; `telegram-group` is not a bus adapter and
uses the ops-alerts group route. Do NOT construct new adapters or
introduce a second recipient config. `NullBusAdapter` (no platform
configured, or under pytest, where `app.py` wires no platform sender) silently drops
the message; the feature self-disables.
The bus adapters are standalone `httpx` clients independent of
`gateway.start()`/`stop()`, so notifications work during early startup
(before the inbound poller is up) and late shutdown (after `gateway.stop()`,
which tears down inbound adapters, not the bus).

**B. Four sites in `app.py`, each in its own try/except — a notification
must NEVER break boot or shutdown.**
- `_on_startup()` top → `notify_lifecycle("starting")`: RECORDS the boot
  (`_record_boot`: reads how the last run ended, then stamps
  `system.lifecycle.last_boot_epoch`); announced only when switched on.
- `_on_startup()` end → `spawn_background(announce_started(
  gateway.connection_report, model=, build=get_build_info()["commit"]))`.
  In the background because it waits (up to `CONNECT_WAIT_S`, 45 s; live
  the adapters connect ~4 s after the gateway starts) for every adapter to
  connect or fail; it gives up when Kazma begins shutting down.
- the gateway-start failure `except` → `startup_failed` (the error as
  `detail`).
- `_on_shutdown()` top → `notify_lifecycle("shutting_down")`: RECORDS the
  stop (`system.lifecycle.last_shutdown_epoch`); announced only when on.
A shutdown stamp at or after the previous boot's = the last run stopped
cleanly ("Down for 34.8 s"; "restarted" within `restart_window_seconds`,
default 60, `0` = no detection); one before it = it did not ("The last run
did not shut down cleanly"). The markers are written whether or not the
event is announced — never gate a stamp on the events list. The downtime
runs to the END OF STARTUP (`announce_started` takes the time before it
waits), never to the send: Slack's 30 s of reconnects turned a 35 s reload
into "started" (live 2026-09-30,
`test_the_wait_for_the_adapters_is_not_downtime`).

**C. An adapter's connection is what its connection said.**
`BaseAdapter.connection_state()` reads the adapter's `ReceiveLog` (§42):
`connected`, `connecting` (with the last problem), `down` (task never
started or ended), `running` (no record). `GatewayManager.connection_report()`
is what the card polls, and `get_status()` (the Gateway Monitor, `kazma
gateway status`) maps the same states -- it used to say "connected" for any
running task.

**D. Config is live-re-read and has a control.**
`get_lifecycle_config()` mirrors `get_hitl_config`/`get_proxy_provider`,
never raises, and is blocking (async callers use `to_thread`). Events
default to `[started, startup_failed]`; an EMPTY list means every message
off; unknown names are logged and ignored (all-unknown = the defaults).
Settings → Alerts → Server status messages writes
`notifications.lifecycle.events` (`PUT /api/settings/alerts`, §33); `PUT /api/settings/single` refuses a name
Kazma does not send (`parse_lifecycle_events`). The old four-event default
pinned in every install's database is retired through §8's
`RETIRED_DEFAULTS`. Tests: `tests/test_lifecycle_start_card.py`.

### 18. Migration System (`kazma-core/kazma_core/migration/`)

A portable-bundle system for moving a full Kazma installation across
machines/OSes (WSL→Windows, Linux→Mac, server→laptop) without the silent
breakage of a naive copy-paste. User surface is the `kazma migrate` CLI
(`export` / `verify` / `import`); the engine lives in
`kazma_core/migration/` so REST/UI can wrap it later.

**Three load-bearing invariants (the whole point of the tool):**

**A. `vault.db` + `KAZMA_VAULT_KEY` travel as an atomic pair.** The vault's
per-installation PBKDF2 salt lives *inside* `vault.db`, so the DB is
undecryptable without its matching key. The bundle carries both: the key in
`meta.env`, a non-reversible fingerprint in `manifest.json`. On import,
`check_vault_key()` (`migration/vault_pairing.py`) compares them: MATCH
proceeds, EMPTY writes the bundle's key, MISMATCH **aborts** unless
`--reset-vault-key` is passed (which backs up the target's existing vault.db
first, then overwrites the key). This is the #1 silent-breakage mode of a
copy-paste migration.

**B. Embedded absolute paths are rewritten to the target root.** A Linux
